¶
{{smaller block|This seal was exhibited to the Heralds at their Visitation of Northants, 1618, "antiquum Sigillum argenteum," and is ''tricked'' in their original MS.
{{right|''Trans. Hist. Soc. of Lancashire and Cheshire'', N. S., V. 33.}}}}

'''trick<sup>4</sup>†''', ''a.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''trig''<sup>1</sup>.

{{smaller block|In two bows that I have, . . . the one is quick of cast, ''trick'', and trim both for pleasure and profit; the other is a lug, slow of cast, following the string, more sure for to last than pleasant for to use.
{{right|''Ascham'', Toxophilus (ed. 1864), p. 14.}}}}

{{smaller block|But tell me, wench, hast done 't so ''trick'' indeed
That heaven itself may wonder at the deed?
{{right|''Peele'', Arraignment of Paris, i. 3.}}}}

'''trick-dagger''' (trik′dag″ėr), ''n.'' A dagger the blade of which slips back into the hilt.

'''tricker<sup>1</sup>''' (trik′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''trick''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''treacher''.] One who tricks; a cheat; a trickster.

'''tricker<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''trigger''.—{{smaller|'''Tricker firelock''', a hand-firearm of the close of the reign of Charles I., so called because discharged by pulling a trigger or tricker. See ''tricker-lock''. ''Jour. Brit. Archæol. Ass.'', XI. 255.}}

'''tricker-lock''' (trik′ėr-lok), ''n.'' A gun-lock arranged with a tricker or trigger of any description. Match-tricker locks and wheel-tricker locks were in use in the seventeenth century.

'''trickery''' (trik′ėr-i), ''n.'' [< ''trick''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ery''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''treachery'' (ME. ''tricherie'', < OF. ''tricherie'', etc.).] The practice of tricks or deceits; artifice; imposture.

streams; drip.

{{smaller block|The three tall fireplaces . . . make one think of the groups that must formerly have gathered there—of all the wet boot-soles, the ''trickling'' doublets, the stiffened fingers, the rheumatic shanks.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 121.}}}}

3. To pass or flow gently like a small stream.

{{smaller block|How fluent nonsense ''trickles'' from his tongue!
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iii. 201.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cause to trickle; pour or shed in small, slow streams.

{{smaller block|With adroit and tender hands they aided the doctor, and ''trickled'' stimulants down her throat.
{{right|''C. Reade'', Hard Cash, xxxvii.}}}}

'''trickle''' (trik′l), ''n.'' [< ''trickle'', ''v.''] 1. A trickling stream; a rill.

{{smaller block|Delicious as ''trickles''
Of wine poured at mass-time.
{{right|''Browning'', Another Way of Love.}}}}

2†. See the quotation.

{{smaller block|''Cacarelle'' [It.], the ''trickles'' or dung of sheepe, goats, rats, or conies.
{{right|''Florio'', 1598.}}}}

'''tricklet''' (trik′let), ''n.'' [< ''trickle'' + ''-et''.] A small, trickling stream; a rill.

{{smaller block|My business lay in the two Anstruthers. A ''tricklet'' of a stream divides them, spanned by a bridge.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Scribner's Mag., IV. 511.}}}}

'''trick-line''' (trik′līn), ''n.'' ''Theat.'', a cord, made very strong and smooth, used in the working of pantomimic changes.

'''trickly'''<sup>1</sup> (trik′li), ''adv.'' [< ''trick''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Neatly; deftly; cleverly.

{{RunningHeader|trick|6471|trickly}}{{smaller block|Several members of Congress had previously complained that the demonetization scheme of 1873 had been pushed surreptitiously through the courses of its passage, Congress having been ''tricked'' into accepting it, doing it scarcely knew what. {{right|''W. Wilson'', Cong. Gov., iii.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To use trickery, deception, or imposture. {{smaller block|Thus they jog on, still ''tricking'', never thriving,
And murdering plays, which still they call reviving.{{right|''Dryden'', To Granville.}}}} '''2.''' To juggle; play. {{smaller block|We may ''trick'' with the word life in its dozen senses until we are weary of ''tricking'', . . . but one fact remains true throughout, . . . that we do not, properly speaking, love life at all, but living. {{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Æs Triplex.}}}} '''3'''†. To toy; handle idly. {{smaller block|The muses forbid that I should restrain your meddling, whom I see already busy with the title and ''tricking'' over the leaves. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, To the Reader.}}}} '''trick'''1 (trik), ''n.'' [< ''trick''1, ''v.''; prob. in part < MD. ''treck'', D. ''trek'', a trick, a pull, draft, etc.: see ''trick''1, ''v.'', and cf. ''track''1.] '''1.''' A crafty or fraudulent device; a deceitful expedient; an artifice; a stratagem. {{smaller block|There is some ''trick'' in this, and you must know it,
And be an agent too.{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, iv. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|But you see they haue some ''trickes'' to cousin God, as before to cousin the Diuell. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 213.}}}} {{smaller block|O, the rare ''tricks'' of a Machiavelian!{{right|''Webster'', White Devil, v. 1.}}}} '''2.''' A feat or an exhibition of skill or dexterity, as in juggling or sleight of hand. {{smaller block|He can do ''tricks'' with his toes, wind silk and thread pearl with them. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Pan's Anniversary.}} Entertain any puppy that comes, like a tumbler, with the same ''tricks'' over and over. {{right|''Congreve'', Old Batchelor, i. 4.}}}} 3. A roguish or mischievous performance; a prank; a practical joke; a hoax. {{smaller block|If I be served such another ''trick'', I'll have my brains ta'en out and buttered, and give them to a dog for a new-year's gift. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 5. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|To play a ''trick'' and make some one or other look foolish was held the most pointed form of wit throughout the back regions of the manor. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xii.}}}} 4. A foolish, vicious, or disgraceful act: with disparaging or contemptuous force. {{smaller block|Didst thou ever see me do such a ''trick?'' {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 4. 43.}}}} {{smaller block|I hope you don't mean to forsake it; that will be but a kind of a mongrel cur's ''trick''. {{right|''Congreve'', Old Batchelor, iv. 5.}}}} 5. A peculiar art; skill; adroitness; knack. {{smaller block|Here 's fine revolution, an we had the ''trick'' to see't. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 1. 99.}}}} {{smaller block|In a little while the ''trick'' of walking on the edge of the water close to the side wall had been learned. {{right|''The Century'', XXXIX. 220.}}}} 6. A peculiar trait, manner, habit, or practice; a characteristic; a peculiarity; a mannerism. {{smaller block|In you a wildness is a noble ''trick'', And cherish'd in ye, and all men must love it. {{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, iii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|What shall I say of the manifold and strange fashions of the garments that are used now-a-days? . . . Sometime we follow the fashion of the Frenchmen. Another time we will have a ''trick'' of the Spaniards. {{right|''Becon'', Early Writings (ed. Parker Soc.), p. 204.}} We've a ''trick'', we young fellows, you may have been told, Of talking (in public) as if we were old. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', The Boys.}}}} 7. A trace; a suggestion; a reminder. {{smaller block|He hath a ''trick'' of Cœur-de-lion's face. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 85.}}}} 8. Something pretended or unreal; a semblance; an illusion. {{smaller block|Truth itself is in her head as dull And useless as a candle in a scull, And all her love of God a groundless claim, A ''trick'' upon the canvas, painted flame. {{right|''Cowper'', Conversation, l. 782.}}}} {{smaller block|In this poor ''trick'' of paint You see the semblance, incomplete and faint, Of the two-fronted Future. {{right|''Whittier'', The Panorama.}}}} 9. Any small article; a toy; a knickknack; a trifle; a trap; a mere nothing: sometimes applied to a child. [Obsolete or provincial U. S.] {{smaller block|Why, 'tis a cockle or a walnut-shell, A knack, a toy, a ''trick'', a baby's cap. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 3. 67.}}}} {{smaller block|The women of this countrey weare aboue an hundreth ''tricks'' and trifles about them. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', II. 64.}}}} {{smaller block|Camp ''tricks'' should be kept in their places, not thrown helter skelter, or left lying where last used. {{right|''Sportsman's Gazetteer'', p. 640.}}}} {{smaller block|Vainly the mother tried to hush the child; the prisoner called out, "Gimme the little ''trick'', Sis; she jes wants to get tuh me." {{right|''The Century'', XL. 219.}}}} 10. In ''card-playing'', the cards collectively which are played in one round. {{smaller|In whist and many other card-games the number of tricks taken makes up the score}} on which the winning or losing of the game depends. A whist trick is complete when the cards are turned and quitted. {{smaller block|Here's a ''trick'' of discarded cards of us! we were rank'd with coats as long as old master lived. {{right|''Middleton, Massinger, and Rowley'', Old Law, iii. 1.}} When in doubt, win the ''trick''. {{right|''Hoyle'', Twenty-four Rules for Beginners, xii.}}}} 11. ''Naut.'', a spell; a turn; the time allotted to a man to stand at the helm, generally two hours. {{smaller block|This night it was my turn to steer, or, as the sailors say, my ''trick'' at the helm, for two hours. {{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 29.}}}} 12. A watch. ''Tuft's Glossary of Thieves' Jargon'' (1798). [Thieves' slang.]{{smaller|—'''The odd trick.''' See ''odd''.—'''To know a trick worth two of that,''' to know of some better contrivance or expedient.}} {{smaller block|Nay, by God, soft; I ''know a trick worth two of that'', i' faith. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 1. 41.}} Hear what he says of you, sir? Clive, best be off to bed, my boy—ho, ho! No, no. We ''know a trick worth two of that.'' {{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, i.}}}} {{smaller|'''To serve one a trick.''' See ''serve''1.—'''Tricks of the trade,''' the expedients, artifices, and dodges of a craft or business; devices or stratagems intended to attract custom or to gain some advantage over one's customers or one's rivals.=='''Syn. 1.''' ''Manœuver, Stratagem'', etc. (see ''artifice''), fraud, imposition, imposture, deception, fetch.}} '''trick2''' (trik), ''v. t.'' [Prob. another use of ''trick''1, ''v.'', as derived from the noun in the sense 'a dexterous artifice,' or 'a touch.' Cf. also ''trick''4. According to some, < W. ''treciaw'', furnish or harness, trick out, < ''trec'', an implement, harness, gear.] To dress; trim; deck; prank; specifically, to arrange, dress, or decorate, especially in a fanciful way, as the person or the hair: often followed by ''out'' or ''up''. {{smaller block|For he [Cato] found not his Country . . . utterly destroyed, but tossed in a dangerous tempest; and being not of authority like the Pilot to take the sterne in hand, and governe the ship, he took himself to ''tricking'' the sailes, and preparing the tackle, so to assist men of greater power. {{right|''North'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 624.}}}} {{smaller block|The Canari put their wiues to the drudgery abroad, whiles themselues spin, weaue, ''tricke vp'' themselues, and performe other womanish functions at home. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 885.}}}} {{smaller block|The women celebrated of old for their beauties yet carry that fame. . . . They have their head ''trickt'' with tassels and flowers. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|A country playhouse, some rude barn ''Tricked out'' for that proud use. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, vii.}}}} '''trick'''3 (trik), ''v. t.'' [< MD. ''trecken'', D. ''trekken'', pull, draw lines, delineate, sketch, = OFries. ''trekka'', ''tregga'', North Fries. ''trecke'', ''tracke'' = LG. ''trekken'' = MHG. ''trecken'' = Dan. ''trække'', draw; a causal form of OHG. ''trehhan'', MHG. ''trechen'', pull, push, shove. From the same source are ult. E. ''track''1, and ''tricker'', now ''trigger''. Cf. also ''trek'' and ''trick''1. This verb seems to have been confused with ''trick''2, deck; cf. ''trickment''.] In ''her.'': (''a'') To draw, as a bearing or a collection of bearings, or a whole escutcheon or achievement of arms. {{smaller|The word implies the representation graphically of armorial bearings in any sense, and should be used instead of ''blazon'', which properly means to describe in words.}} {{smaller block|They are blazoned there; there they are ''tricked'', they and their pedigrees. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}} (''b'') Especially, to draw in black and white only, without color, or to sketch slightly, whether a bearing or a whole achievement. {{smaller block|This seal was exhibited to the Heralds at their Visitation of Northants, 1618, "antiquum Sigillum argenteum," and is ''tricked'' in their original MS. {{right|''Trans. Hist. Soc. of Lancashire and Cheshire'', N. S., V. 33.}}}} '''trick4†''', ''a.'' and ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''trig''1. {{smaller block|In two bows that I have, . . . the one is quick of cast, ''trick'', and trim both for pleasure and profit; the other is a lug, slow of cast, following the string, more sure for to last than pleasant for to use. {{right|''Ascham'', Toxophilus (ed. 1864), p. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|But tell me, wench, hast done 't so ''trick'' indeed That heaven itself may wonder at the deed? {{right|''Peele'', Arraignment of Paris, i. 3.}}}} '''trick-dagger''' (trik′dag″ėr), ''n.'' A dagger the blade of which slips back into the hilt. '''tricker1''' (trik′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''trick''1 + ''-er''1. Cf. ''treacher''.] One who tricks; a cheat; a trickster. '''tricker2†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''trigger''.—{{smaller|'''Tricker firelock''', a hand-firearm of the close of the reign of Charles I., so called because discharged by pulling a trigger or tricker. See ''tricker-lock''. ''Jour. Brit. Archæol. Ass.'', XI. 255.}} '''tricker-lock''' (trik′ėr-lok), ''n.'' A gun-lock arranged with a tricker or trigger of any description. Match-tricker locks and wheel-tricker locks were in use in the seventeenth century. '''trickery''' (trik′ėr-i), ''n.'' [< ''trick''1 + ''-ery''1. Cf. ''treachery'' (ME. ''tricherie'', < OF. ''tricherie'', etc.).] The practice of tricks or deceits; artifice; imposture. {{smaller block|The nomination-day was a great epoch of successful ''trickery'', or, to speak in a more Parliamentary manner, of war stratagem, on the part of skilful agents. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xxx.}}}} '''trickily''' (trik′i-li), ''adv.'' In a tricky manner; trickishly. '''trickiness''' (trik′i-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being tricky or trickish; trickishness. {{smaller block|The right of the blind to ask charity lapses if it becomes a mere business and with all the ''trickiness'' by which a street business is sometimes characterised. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 396.}}}} '''tricking1''' (trik′ing), ''p. a.'' [Ppr. of ''trick''1, ''v.''] Practising or playing tricks; tricky; deceitful; artful. {{smaller block|Go get thee gone, and by thyself Devise some ''tricking'' game. {{right|''Robin Hood and the Golden Arrow'' (Child's Ballads, V. 383).}}}} {{smaller block|We presently discovered that they were as expert thieves, and as ''tricking'' in their exchanges, as any people we had yet met with. {{right|''Cook'', Second Voyage, ii. 7.}}}} '''tricking2''' (trik′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''trick''2, ''v.''] Articles of outfit; appurtenances, especially ornamental trifles. {{smaller block|Go get us properties, And ''tricking'' for our fairies. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 4. 78.}}}} '''tricking3''' (trik′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''trick''3, ''v.''] In ''her.'', a graphic representation of heraldic bearings or an entire achievement. See ''trick''3. {{smaller block|Arms verbally and technically described are blazoned; the verbal description is the blazon; if they are drawn in pen or pencil in monochrome, showing the lines of tincture, they are said to be "tricked"; such a drawing is a ''tricking;'' if they are given in gold and colours, they are illuminated or painted. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., V. 414.}}}} '''trickish''' (trik′ish), ''a.'' [< ''trick''1 + ''-ish''1.] Given to or characterized by trickery; deceitful; artful. {{smaller block|So loose and slippery and ''trickish'' way of reasoning. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', To Pope, March 26, 1721.}}}} {{smaller block|The chimpanzee . . . is extremely kind to children, showing no ''trickish'' or malicious temper, even endeavoring to amuse them, and induce them to play. {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XIII. 435.}}}} =Syn. Deceptive, roguish. {{smaller|See ''cunning''1.}} '''trickishly''' (trik′ish-li), ''adv.'' In a trickish manner; artfully; deceitfully. '''trickishness''' (trik′ish-nes), ''n.'' The state of being trickish, deceitful, or artful. {{smaller block|Charges of duplicity, management, artifice, and ''trickishness.'' {{right|''V. Knox'', Winter Evenings, xxiv.}}}} '''trickle''' (trik′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''trickled'', ppr. ''trickling.'' [< ME. ''triklen, trikilen, trekelen;'' prob. a var. of ''striklen'' (with which it interchanges), trickle, freq. of ''striken'', rarely ME. ''triken'', go: see ''strike.'' In mod. times the word has been regarded as connected with ''trill''1. Cf. Sc. ''trinkle'', also ''trintle'', trickle.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To flow in a small interrupted stream; run down in drops: as, water ''trickles'' from the eaves. {{smaller block|The red blode ''triklond'' to his knee. {{right|''MS. Cantab.'' Ff. v. 48, f. 122. (''Halliwell.'')}}}} {{smaller block|Nay! ful of sorowe thou now me seest;
The teeris ''trikilen'' dowun on my face,
For "filius regis mortuus est." {{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 207.}}}} '''2.''' To let fall a liquid in drops or small broken streams; drip. {{smaller block|The three tall fireplaces . . . make one think of the groups that must formerly have gathered there—of all the wet boot-soles, the ''trickling'' doublets, the stiffened fingers, the rheumatic shanks. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 121.}}}} 3. To pass or flow gently like a small stream. {{smaller block|How fluent nonsense ''trickles'' from his tongue! {{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iii. 201.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' To cause to trickle; pour or shed in small, slow streams. {{smaller block|With adroit and tender hands they aided the doctor, and ''trickled'' stimulants down her throat. {{right|''C. Reade'', Hard Cash, xxxvii.}}}} '''trickle''' (trik′l), ''n.'' [< ''trickle'', ''v.''] 1. A trickling stream; a rill. {{smaller block|Delicious as ''trickles'' Of wine poured at mass-time. {{right|''Browning'', Another Way of Love.}}}} 2†. See the quotation. {{smaller block|''Cacarelle'' [It.], the ''trickles'' or dung of sheepe, goats, rats, or conies. {{right|''Florio'', 1598.}}}} '''tricklet''' (trik′let), ''n.'' [< ''trickle'' + ''-et''.] A small, trickling stream; a rill. {{smaller block|My business lay in the two Anstruthers. A ''tricklet'' of a stream divides them, spanned by a bridge. {{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Scribner's Mag., IV. 511.}}}} '''trick-line''' (trik′līn), ''n.'' ''Theat.'', a cord, made very strong and smooth, used in the working of pantomimic changes. '''trickly'''1 (trik′li), ''adv.'' [< ''trick''1 + ''-ly''2.] Neatly; deftly; cleverly.
